subject: vinegaroon
title: This Desert Arachnid Sprays Acid 16 Times Stronger Than Vinegar

scenes.text: This creature smells like a salad. Get closer and you'll regret it.
The vinegaroon looks like a scorpion crossed with a lobster: palm-sized, black, with a thin whip for a tail. No venom at all.
Grab it and the base of that tail swivels toward you and fires a mist from two glands.
The mist is 85 percent acetic acid, the stuff in vinegar. Salad vinegar is about five percent. This is sixteen times stronger.
It can fire five times before the glands run dry. Skunks, coyotes and raccoons take a face full and give up.
Then it goes back to hunting scorpions and cockroaches. The arachnid that beats predators with the kitchen cupboard.

description:
The vinegaroon, or giant whip scorpion, of the American Southwest has no venom. Instead it defends itself with a spray that is 85 percent acetic acid, the compound in vinegar, which is about 5 percent, so roughly 16 times stronger.
Two glands at the base of its flexible tail aim the spray in any direction, and an adult can fire about five times before they refill. Texas A&M AgriLife Extension says it is harmless to people and eats scorpions, cockroaches, crickets and millipedes.
Would you keep one in your garden? Comment below.
first_comment: It hunts by feeling vibrations through its long front legs, which work like antennae, not legs. Which animal with a chemical weapon should we cover next?
